This work addresses the challenge of estimating the mean of a population that is partially unknown, a scenario often arising in sampling where only a subset of the population is accessible. We propose a generalized maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) designed to infer the global mean from data drawn from a mixture distribution, utilizing available samples from one or more component distributions. We establish the consistency of this estimator and derive its asymptotic distribution. Furthermore, we evaluate the method's performance through a simulation study and demonstrate its practical utility with a real-world example.

Knowledge tracing (KT) is a series of techniques designed to model and forecast a learner's proficiency by analyzing their exercise history. Over the last few years, numerous research groups have developed various deep learning-based approaches for these tasks. However, a significant gap exists in the availability of standardized tools to assess, compare, and validate these deep learning knowledge tracing models. To address this issue, we have created pyKT, an open-source Python library that facilitates the evaluation of multiple leading knowledge tracing models. This tool enables researchers to efficiently test various models on their datasets and compare results using shared evaluation metrics. Furthermore, pyKT supports the generation of synthetic data based on specific rules to rigorously evaluate model performance through rule-based benchmarks. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of this library by utilizing pyKT to evaluate several prominent models.

This work demonstrates that an elliptic, second-order differential operator $P$ defined on a Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ possesses a closed range if and only if its associated operator on $\mathbb{R}^n \setminus K$ (where $K$ is a compact set) also has a closed range. As a corollary, we establish that $P$ has a closed range on $\mathbb{R}^n$ precisely when it does so on $\mathbb{R}^n \setminus K$ for some compact $K$. Furthermore, we prove that $P$ fails to have a closed range on $\mathbb{R}^n \setminus K$ whenever $P$ admits a non-trivial element in its null space supported entirely within $K$. Finally, these findings are utilized to deliver a streamlined demonstration of a result originally by B. Helffer and J. Sjöstrand, confirming that $P$ has a closed range on every open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with a compact boundary.

This work introduces a proposal for a uniform, extensible interface designed to support various Solvers. The suggested format is structured to be easily understood and allows for the straightforward integration of new solver-specific features. It supports the generation of machine-readable files, which have already been implemented within the Coq toolchain. Furthermore, this implementation includes a corresponding Coq library dedicated to the parsing and validation of the format.

In traditional centralized deep learning, training relies on vast datasets and massive computational power, which can be augmented by ensembling multiple models. Conversely, privacy concerns and the prohibitive cost of data transfer prevent such ensembling in federated learning (FL), where training occurs across distributed devices using local information. Although asynchronous updates are a common feature of centralized training, existing FL approaches are restricted to synchronous aggregations. This limitation creates a significant performance gap, as asynchronous methods can utilize unrestricted model gradients, whereas synchronous methods suffer gradient restrictions due to the need for synchronized completion. To address this, we propose Buffered-FL, a new framework that enables asynchronous aggregations in FL. Our approach allows clients to upload models immediately after updating them, regardless of training completion status, while the server manages updates by maintaining a buffer and aggregating models periodically. We demonstrate that Buffered-FL achieves convergence rates comparable to centralized training, even when clients upload models containing only partial layers.

This study evaluates and compares cross-lingual transfer learning and coarse-to-fine training methods for low-resource automatic speech recognition (ASR) using the Czech-English CTS dataset. The Czech-English CTS dataset, comprising 1,000 hours of Czech and English audio, was created to support Czech-English ASR translation. The paper presents a new Czech-English ASR translation system based on these learning strategies.

Node embedding is a machine learning technique designed to represent graph nodes as low-dimensional vectors, capturing the inherent characteristics of the network. This approach has been applied to diverse fields, including social media analysis, recommendation systems, and knowledge graph question answering. This paper introduces "Twitch Players," a dataset derived from Twitch streams to assess proximity-preserving and structural role-based node embedding models. We evaluate five proximity-preserving algorithms and three structural role-based algorithms using five distinct metrics. Our findings indicate that the "DeepWalk" algorithm and the "Structural2Vec" model perform most effectively across the tested metrics. Furthermore, we analyze the learned vector representations to assess their ability to capture semantic information within the data.

The $\rho^0(1450)$ resonance, a vector meson with quantum numbers $J^{PC}=1^{--}$ and mass near 1.45 GeV/$c^2$, has been observed in $B$-meson decays into two kaons ($B\to \bar{K}K\rho^0\to \bar{K}K\pi^+\pi^-$) via the intermediate $f_X(1500)$ state. This analysis utilized a dataset of $1.0$ fb$^{-1}$ collected by the Belle II detector at the KEKB asymmetric $e^+e^-$ energy operating at the $\Upsilon(4S)$ resonance. The study presents the first measurement of the branching fraction for $B^0\to \bar{K}^0K^0f_X(1500)$, determined to be $(1.0\pm 0.2\pm 0.2)\times 10^{-4}$, where the first uncertainty is statistical and the second is systematic. Furthermore, branching fractions for the $B^0\to \bar{K}^0K^0\rho^0(1450)$ and $B^+\to \bar{K}^0K^+\rho^0(1450)$ modes are reported for the first time, with values of $(1.0\

We propose that a significant fraction of the dark sector consists of primordial black holes (PBHs) formed during the early universe. This formation occurs because cosmological fluctuations were amplified to levels far exceeding those observed today, likely due to the influence of primordial scalar fields. This PBH population generates a dark dimension, defined by a metric where the radial coordinate represents the logarithm of the mass of the black holes located at that radius. We demonstrate that this dark dimension possesses a well-defined event horizon, which functions as a holographic boundary separating the universe into two regions: an external bulk containing the PBHs and an internal AdS-like space. We further show that this setup aligns with the recent Witten conjecture regarding the swampland, which posits that every consistent theory of quantum gravity must admit a corresponding dark dimension. Finally, we suggest that the formation of these PBHs could explain the enigmatic dark substance fraction composed of these early-universe remnants.

Series elastic actuators (SEAs) are increasingly utilized in mobile robotics to enhance safety and compliance, yet their precise force regulation remains challenging due to force measurement noise and dynamic transmission force variations. To address this, this study introduces a novel, high-bandwidth force estimation framework that integrates a transmission force observer (TFO) with a series elastic transmission (SET) model. A key innovation is the use of a robust differentiator to process SEA dynamics, enabling accurate derivation of transmission acceleration from acceleration sensor data despite inherent noise. By using this acceleration to estimate the derivative of the transmission velocity, the proposed SET model effectively captures force transmission dynamics. Experimental results on a physical SEA platform demonstrate that this framework significantly outperforms conventional force estimation methods in terms of accuracy and bandwidth. Consequently, this high-performance model supports robust force control, facilitating safer human-robot interaction and more versatile collaborative tasks.

This study examines a model of self-driven particles, known as racers, which move at a constant speed and reorient randomly upon encountering neighbors. We observe that these agents spontaneously organize into gaps of fixed size, forming structures like rafts and rings. The work derives the probability distribution for gap sizes and analyzes the dynamics of ring expansion and contraction. Additionally, the research investigates the structural properties of rafts and rings, comparing them to one-dimensional and two-dimensional self-driven systems.

We investigate the phase diagram of SU(Nc) gauge theories in three dimensions, focusing on lattice formulations that incorporate multistate scalar fields with multiple independent parameters. By utilizing mean-field analysis, we identify both the second-order transition separating the confining and Higgs phases and the second-order transition separating distinct Higgs phases. Our findings demonstrate that the locations of these phase boundaries are governed by the specific parameters defining the scalar field. Furthermore, we examine the masses of relevant excitations near these transitions. In particular, we analyze the behavior of the Higgs mode and the mode associated with the phase transition between the confining and Higgs sectors, as well as the phase transition mode between two Higgs phases.

This study introduces a Temporal Difference learning framework enhanced with Gaussian Process interpolation to create an efficient framework for marine robot navigation. While traditional Temporal Difference methods rely on interpolating data points to estimate value functions, this new approach interpolates the policy function directly. By interpolating the policy, the system can determine actions for any state within the interpolation domain, allowing the robot to execute tasks even when encountering states not yet encountered during training. This capability is critical for autonomous marine operations, where navigating uncharted waters is essential.

Linear arrangement is a fundamental graph theory problem that seeks a one-to-one mapping of vertices to integer coordinates to minimize the largest distance between adjacent values. For decades, researchers have investigated the linear arrangements of specific graph families, such as trees and grids. In this study, we introduce a constant-depth arranging algorithm applicable to all binary-arity trees. This algorithm operates within an arranging algorithm framework that functions as a synchronous, local, message-passing process. By utilizing this method, we achieve an optimal arrangement for all $n$-vertex binary-arity trees within constant circuit depth, specifically $O(\log n)$ depth.

We analyze the equilibrium of static, spherically symmetric stellar systems composed of dual fluids with anisotropy in both the Schwarzschild and Kerr-Newman spacetimes. Within the Einstein field equations, we derive the exact solutions for the Tolman IV interior metric by imposing specific constraints on the equation of state and anisotropy. Furthermore, we establish the necessary boundary and junction conditions to ensure a smooth transition to the exterior Schwarzschild metric. Finally, we numerically evaluate the physical viability of these solutions. Our findings indicate that the derived models satisfy all required physical conditions and are consistent with observational data.

We present a novel numerical model for the formation of multi-armed spiral structures in multi-component galaxies. This approach integrates the fast multipole method (FMM) to solve the Poisson equation, enabling the simulation of gravitational interactions between dark matter, gas, and stellar populations. Our framework employs a two-phase strategy: a coarse grid phase captures global dynamics across the entire system, followed by a fine grid phase that refines details within specific regions of interest.

Our simulations feature a dark matter halo, a stellar disk divided into a bulge and an exponential outer component, along with a central starburst ring and an outer spiral arm. We specifically investigate the orbital evolution of the starburst ring under the gravitational influence of the outer arm and the central bar. Our findings indicate that the bar drives a resonance within the ring, which facilitates the formation of the multi-armed spiral pattern. Additionally, we demonstrate that the outer arm exerts a stabilizing effect on the ring, preventing uncontrolled winding and promoting structural longevity. These results suggest that our FMM-based modeling approach offers a robust method for simulating complex multi-component galaxies and accurately reproducing their observed spiral designs.

We investigate the impact of magnetic fields on the evolution of gas and stellar discs during galaxy mergers, utilizing a fully three-dimensional, fully relativistic, and fully coupled magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulation framework. Our study focuses on a gas-rich merger between two galaxies of equal mass, examining scenarios with varying initial magnetic field strengths and orientations. We find that while fields of microgauss strength significantly influence the structural evolution of both gas and stars, the specific effects depend heavily on the field's orientation. In cases where the field is aligned parallel to the galactic disc, magnetic fields suppress the formation of giant elliptical galaxies by inhibiting the rapid coalescence of stellar discs. Conversely, when the field is oriented perpendicular to the disc, magnetic fields accelerate the formation of giant ellipticals by facilitating the swift dissipation of residual angular momentum within the merging systems.

This paper introduces Infection-aware Contrastive Mixup Classification (ICMC), a novel framework designed to enhance COVID-19 severity classification. We address the challenge of limited labeled data by leveraging the abundance of unlabeled samples through self-training. Specifically, we employ a contrastive learning framework to automatically generate pseudo-labels for these unlabeled datasets. Building on this foundation, we utilize a mixup strategy to create augmented training samples. These techniques are implemented in two stages: first, an initial model is trained on pseudo-labeled data to establish a robust baseline, and subsequently, a refined model is developed using these pseudo-labels refined via self-training outputs. Comprehensive experiments conducted on the COVID-19 CT Scan dataset confirm that our approach significantly improves the performance of COVID-19 severity identification.

Grammatical error correction (GEC) has predominantly relied on deep learning models trained on extensive datasets like TED-Lium1 and TREC, which have enabled high accuracy. However, these models typically exhibit poor performance when applied to new domains without additional training data. To address this limitation, we introduce a new dataset named "TUM-GEC1," comprising 1,000 error-ridden sentences and their corrections annotated by native speakers for the domain of informal written German chat. This dataset is designed to support few-shot learning. Furthermore, we propose a meta-learning framework that trains on multiple source domains to adapt to TUM-GEC1 with minimal data. Our approach achieves a WER of 21.0% using only 100 training sentences, outperforming a model trained on the large-scale Lium1 dataset, which reached a WER of 21.6% with 1,000 sentences from the target domain.

Rounding is a ubiquitous practice in daily life and professional settings, yet it introduces ambiguity when averaging discrete data to derive an integer count. For instance, a mean of 2.6 or 2.4 from a dataset should both round to 3, but the latter value technically represents a count of either 2 or 3. This study examines the implications of this inherent uncertainty for statistical inference. We propose a Bayesian framework that incorporates this ambiguity by assigning a uniform prior over the two plausible integer values associated with any given rounded mean. Consequently, this approach yields a posterior distribution for the count that is shifted relative to the standard method of simply rounding the sample mean.

We report on the magnetic properties of GdInO$_3$ single crystals, which feature a honeycomb lattice of Gd atoms. Our findings reveal a three-dimensional honeycomb structure with Gd atoms occupying the A2$_{1}$am space group, where Gd moments are antiferromagnetically aligned along the c-axis and exhibit honeycomb ordering within the ab-planes. Furthermore, we observed that the Gd magnetic anisotropy is significantly enhanced by the crystal field environment.

We investigate the allocation of indivisible goods among agents with varying valuations, focusing on strategic behavior, fairness, and efficiency. Specifically, we examine the Pure Nash Equilibria (PNE) within this framework and evaluate how PNE allocations align with established fairness and efficiency metrics. Our analysis reveals that in environments where each agent receives at least one item, PNE guarantees every agent an item valued at least half as highly as their most preferred available option; conversely, if some agents receive nothing, the lower bound for this fraction drops to one-third. We further demonstrate that Pareto efficiency is not assured in PNE outcomes by constructing a scenario where a more efficient allocation exists yet remains unreachable from a PNE state. However, we identify a sufficient condition under which a Pareto improvement is always feasible from any PNE. Finally, we establish that the Minimum Envy ratio is bounded below by $1/2$ in cases where all but one agent obtain an item, while the bound tightens to $1/3$ if any agent receives nothing.

Gan-based methods have become a dominant approach for unsupervised image style transfer and domain adaptation, largely due to their ability to learn deterministic mappings through mode collapse. However, this rigidity causes the generator to map diverse source images identically, ignoring image-specific attributes and resulting in a lack of diversity. To address this, we introduce a stochastic conversion framework that integrates a noise vector into the mapping process to ensure varied outputs for the same source content. This model is trained using a combination of domain adversarial and cycle-consistency losses, enhanced by a novel diversity loss that promotes variation among converted images. Experiments demonstrate that this technique surpasses current state-of-the-art results in both domain adaptation and style transfer tasks.

We present a new kinematic analysis of the spiral galaxy UGC 8839, revealing a prominent, hyper-stable disk anomaly. This feature exhibits a flat rotation curve and a spin direction opposite to the main galaxy body, yet maintains a vertical alignment with the primary disk. The anomaly's low velocity dispersion and the lack of significant misalignment suggest it is not a satellite system. Instead, we propose that this structure is a massive, in-situ disk resulting from a major merger event. This scenario involves the accretion of a counter-rotating disk that was sufficiently massive to retain its structural integrity and kinematic identity, avoiding complete mixing with the host galaxy.

Paleo-detectors represent a proposed frontier in dark matter research, utilizing rock samples to search for microscopic damage tracks generated by dark matter scattering events. This study presents updated projections for various detector technologies, incorporating refined estimates for background noise and dark matter flux. Additionally, we introduce a novel methodology to forecast the sensitivity of these devices to dark matter candidates that evade current constraints from direct detection experiments.

This paper introduces a novel update mechanism for encrypted databases that leverages update-specific differential privacy to conceal data modification patterns. In this approach, the privacy parameter $\epsilon$ is applied to each individual update, ensuring that an adversary cannot discern whether a specific data element was altered. This method is versatile, supporting various types of database updates, and is implemented as an extension to the R* structure within the BAE-DB encrypted database framework. The proposed DP-Sync mechanism was evaluated through extensive experiments, demonstrating that it successfully obscures update behaviors while maintaining efficient query performance.

Although Random Forest (RF) is a popular choice for both classification and regression tasks, developing effective methods to evaluate the importance of features remains challenging. This paper introduces a novel feature significance metric grounded in Maximum Utilization Coefficient (MUC). The proposed approach evaluates feature importance by analyzing the extent to which features are leveraged across the entire forest, specifically examining their utilization within individual decision trees. By incorporating the proposed MUC-based metric into an adversarial analysis framework, we evaluate the performance of our RF model. The results indicate that the proposed method outperforms existing feature selection techniques. Furthermore, the study reveals that the proposed approach effectively distinguifies the roles of features in a well-tuned Random Forest classifier.

Surgical instrument segmentation is a vital computer-aided technique designed to enhance surgical precision and efficiency. This study introduces a new deep learning architecture, known as the Multi-Scale Attention U-Net (MSA-U-Net), specifically for segmenting surgical tools in laparoscopic videos. The proposed model integrates Convolutional Block Attention Mechanisms (CBAM) into the encoder-decoder framework of U-Net. By applying channel and spatial attention mechanisms, the MSA-UNet enables the network to prioritize relevant features while suppressing irrelevant background information. Furthermore, the integration of CBAM facilitates the extraction of features across multiple scales, allowing the model to effectively capture both fine-grained details and broader contextual patterns. The MSA-U-Net was evaluated against two established baselines: the original U-Net and the Attention U-Net (A-U-Net). The evaluation utilized two datasets: the SICK-Bench dataset, comprising 1,000 annotated still images, and the SiLVS dataset, a collection of 1,000 annotated surgical videos. Quantitative assessments included the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) and the 95th percentile of the 95th percentile of the 95th percentile of the 95th percentile of the 95th percentile of the 95th percentile of the 95th percentile of the 95th percentile of the 95th percentile of the 95th

This paper introduces a novel unsupervised individual Re-Identification (ReID) method designed to extract discriminative features from video streams containing numerous pedestrians. Unlike supervised approaches, this method requires no labeled data, thereby eliminating the labor-intensive annotation process. It employs a self-supervised contrastive learning framework that generates identity-aware representations through identity-agnostic pre-training. Specifically, we utilize a batch-level negative mining strategy to construct positive-negative image pairs within each training batch. Additionally, we propose an iterative refinement approach that enhances the quality of generated labels through successive training cycles. Extensive experiments conducted on the VIPoR, iLIDS-NC, and Market-1501 datasets demonstrate that this method significantly outperforms existing unsupervised ReID techniques.

This paper introduces a new realizations-threshold based GARCH model designed to estimate the conditional value-at-risk (VaR) for financial assets. The proposed framework integrates a threshold mechanism that defines conditional first- and second-order moments, utilizing the realized threshold estimated through the realized range. Empirical analysis using daily data for the S&P 500, Nasdaq 100, and Dow Jones Industrial averages from 1990 to 2019 demonstrates that the new model outperforms standard GARCH specifications in forecasting tail risk.

We introduce a robust method for estimating the mean and covariance of a parameter vector $\mathbf{x}$, utilizing a sample of $N$ independent realizations $\mathbf{x}_i$ drawn from an underlying distribution. This approach remains effective even when the data contains outliers or deviates from normality. In the context of pulsar timing residuals, we apply this method to infer the mean and covariance of the parameters $\mathbf{x}$, which characterize the distribution of those residuals.

We examine pion states with two current insertions on the lattice to uncover the underlying structure of the resulting states. By analyzing the spatial dependence of these states, we determine that the two current components exhibit a relative twist of $\pi$. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the states' spatial extent is governed by the more expansive current among the pair.

We present a comprehensive analysis of the optical and near-infrared variability of T Tauri star XX Cha, utilizing archival data from the ESO archive and new observations from the ESO Very Large Telescope. XX Cha exhibits a complex variability pattern characterized by a long-term trend, superimposed with mid-term oscillations and short-term fluctuations. Over a 20-year baseline, XX Cha's mean optical brightness has declined by approximately 0.25 magnitudes, while its mean near-infrared flux has dropped by roughly 0.15 dex. This decline is accompanied by a decrease in the star's intrinsic color, indicating a reduction in accretion rate by a factor of 2 to 3. Furthermore, XX Cha displays a distinct behavior in its H-alpha emission line, which has weakened significantly over the last decade. Our findings reveal that XX Cha's accretion rate has fluctuated across a wide spectrum, ranging from $10^{-7}$ to $10^{-9}$ M$_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$. We suggest that stars like XX Cha, which exhibit such extreme variability, are likely responsible for the observed dispersion in accretion rates among other T Tauri stars.

This study examines how individuals respond to shifts in the fairness of opportunity regarding the redistribution of earnings. We observe that people adjust their choices based on how redistribution alters the equality of chance, a reaction that standard models ignoring fairness often fail to capture. By integrating this behavior into a framework featuring transferable utility and the allocation of a divisible good, we analyze how it influences the redistribution of income. Our findings indicate that when the opportunity structure becomes more equitable, a greater proportion of individuals support the redistribution of income. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the magnitude of this effect varies depending on whether the good is consumed in identical or heterogeneous forms.

This paper introduces the definition of quantum $A$-hypergeometric series for a given algebraic variety $X$ and a line bundle $L$ over $X$, generalizing the quantum $K$ theory first developed by Galkin and Sheshadri. The author demonstrates that these series are invariant under isomorphisms of pairs $(X,L)$, mirroring a property observed in classical $K$ theory. Furthermore, the paper establishes a $V$-stationarity condition applicable to the general quantum $A$-hypergeometric series and confirms the existence of a virtual quantum $K$ theory for a variety $X$ equipped with a very ample line bundle $L$.

In machine learning, the quality of data and models is inextricably linked, making it essential to identify and rectify data issues within the broader context of the entire pipeline. We introduce a novel framework for diagnosing data anomalies that leverages Shapley values to evaluate an observation's contribution to a model's output. By integrating this framework with a machine learning pipeline, we can pinpoint the root causes of label errors and uncover intricate correlations between features and targets. We validate our approach using both real-world and synthetic datasets, demonstrating that our method surpasses existing techniques in pinpointing label faults and revealing hidden patterns.

The origins of radio sources in Galactic globular clusters (GCs) are categorized into two groups: those driven by stellar dynamics and those fueled by stellar mass loss. This study aims to determine which mechanism predominates by analyzing the radio emission from 10 GCs with varying degrees of core compactness. Utilizing the MAVERIC survey, we conducted deep 21-cm observations with the Green Bank Telescope, achieving a sensitivity of approximately 100 $\mu$Jy. Our survey successfully identified 10 new radio sources, bringing the total known population in GCs to 20. We discovered a strong correlation between radio luminosity and core compactness, noting that the most luminous sources reside in the most compact cores. This finding supports the hypothesis that radio emission is primarily generated by the dynamical interactions of stars.

We introduce a novel algorithm for reconstructing an unknown hypergraph from its partial knowledge. This approach is applicable to both fully and partially observed hyperedges. The method is grounded in a new concept called the "incidence matrix of a hyperedge," which serves as a generalized representation of the subhyperedge incident to a specific vertex. The proposed algorithm functions by iteratively identifying hyperedges through the intersection of their respective incidence matrices. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the algorithm is guaranteed to succeed when all hyperedges are known. Furthermore, in scenarios where only a subset of hyperedges is observable, the algorithm recovers the correct structure with high probability, provided the known hyperedges constitute a sufficiently large random sample. Numerical experiments confirm the algorithm's strong empirical performance.

The research investigates the influence of directional emission on laser light within a microcavity possessing a parabolic potential, focusing on how entropy production varies as the emission directionality shifts. By calculating the rate of entropy generation, the study reveals that maximizing directionality does not necessarily minimize it; instead, the lowest generation occurs when the directionality is moderate. Furthermore, the findings indicate that the linear response regime is reached when directionality reaches a value of approximately 0.5.

We examine the non-Markovian dynamics of a two-level atom interacting with a thermal ensemble via spontaneous Raman scattering, utilizing a reduced density matrix approach to derive an approximate analytical solution. Our results demonstrate that the atom's interaction with the radiation field modifies the statistics of photons emitted in the direction of the incident laser. Specifically, we identify a non-linear, collective impact arising from the atom-field coupling that enhances single-photon emission. Furthermore, we show that cooling the atomic ensemble further accentuates this effect, thereby offering a pathway to generate single-photon states using only thermal resources.

Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) focuses on learning effective joint behavior policies from historical data collected by multiple agents. A primary challenge in this domain is ensuring that new, useful trajectories are generated by combining existing data points. In this study, we introduce a novel offline multi-agent algorithm that creates new trajectories by linking segments of existing ones. Unlike previous offline MARL approaches, which often struggle with data diversity and suboptimal path formation, our method specifically targets the creation of high-quality routes. We provide strong theoretical backing for our approach, demonstrating that it achieves a sample complexity of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(SAR\frac{SAK\sqrt{H|{\mathcal{O}}|\Sigma\bar{\Sigma}}}{\epsilon})$, where $K$ represents the number of agents. Here, $S$ and $A$ denote the number of states and actions per agent, $H$ is the task horizon, $\epsilon$ is the sub-optimality gap, and $\bar{\Sigma}$ is the maximum sub-optimality of the constructed new trajectories. Extensive experiments confirm that our algorithm significantly outperforms existing offline MARL methods.

This study introduces a convolutional neural network designed to register megavoltage computed tomography (MVCT) images acquired at the linear accelerator treatment room with corresponding three-dimensional (3D) CT scans. While conventional registration methods have been adapted for this purpose, they often require substantial manual intervention and are prone to inaccuracies. Our proposed approach automates the registration process, delivering rapid and precise alignment. The architecture employs a fully convolutional encoder-decoder framework to predict a dense displacement field, which is then applied to transform the MVCT images. To generate the necessary training data, a previously developed automatic MVCT reconstruction algorithm was utilized to create synthetic views from 3D CT scans, establishing paired training sets. Additionally, a loss function was devised to account for the sparse sampling inherent in MVCT data. Experiments indicate that the registration method achieves a mean target registration error of 1.5 mm across ten patients, with a mean computation time of 0.4 seconds per image.

The concept of single-particle entanglement, introduced over a decade ago, has recently gained traction in both theoretical and experimental research. In this work, we demonstrate that single-particle entanglement enables access to genuinely new physical phenomena, specifically by enabling states of one system to be conditioned into states of spatially distant systems without direct interaction. We establish a rigorous definition of single-particle steering and illustrate its presence in various scenarios. We further argue that single-particle steering constitutes a distinct resource from both standard discrete and continuous variable multipartite steering. Finally, we show that single-particle steering produces effects that defy explanation via local operations and single-particle measurements, thereby encompassing phenomena beyond the reach of nonlocal models involving pre-existing local hidden states.

The integration of Blockchain technology within Federated Learning frameworks for Internet of Vehicles is proposed to address security and trust challenges. This review examines existing literature on Blockchain-enabled FL for IoVs, categorizing it into two main groups: those utilizing a Proof-of-Work (PoW) consensus mechanism and those employing Proof-of-Authorization (PoA). This categorization facilitates a comparative analysis of current solutions, offering insights that can guide future research and development efforts.

We report the detection of gamma-ray emission from V392 Persei, a known dwarf nova, during its 2012 nova eruption. This event marks the first observation of gamma-ray radiation from a nova eruption originating in a dwarf nova system. Our findings indicate that the peak gamma-ray luminosity reached approximately $1.1 \times 10^{37}$ erg s$^{-1}$, with a peak gamma-ray energy of $1.1 \times 10^{37}$ erg s$^{-1}$, and a peak gamma-ray luminosity of $1.1 \times 10^{37}$ erg s$^{-1}$, and a peak gamma-ray luminosity of $1.1 \times 10^{37}$ erg s$^{-1}$, and a peak gamma-ray luminosity of $1.1 \times 10^{37}$ erg s$^{-1}$, and a peak gamma-ray luminosity of $1.1 \times 10^{37}$ erg s$^{-1}$, and a peak gamma-ray luminosity of $1.1 \times 10^{37}$ erg s$^{-1}$, and a peak gamma-ray luminosity of $1.1 \times 10^{37}$ erg s$^{-1}$, and a peak gamma-ray luminosity of $1.1 \times 10^{37}$

Topologically ordered systems are recognized for their potential to protect quantum information and facilitate computing. A key feature enabling this is the ability to execute topologically non-trivial operations, which correspond to logical gates, through braiding and fusion of anyons. This study presents a comparison of gate implementations derived from braiding two-qubit versus multi-qubit anyons within the toric code. We demonstrate that while both methods can achieve universal computation, the two-qubit approach offers a distinct advantage: it enables the implementation of Clifford gates via operations that are topologically trivial.

This study evaluates the performance of a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) codebook generation method and compares it against the conventional $k$-means approach. The proposed GMM framework involves initializing a codebook with randomly selected vectors, where each vector is associated with a specific Gaussian component. During iterations, the algorithm updates both the codebook Gaussians and the assignment of training data points. Once convergence is achieved, the codebook is finalized. This proposed method is implemented within a feedback encoding scheme for the downlink physical layer of FDD LTE, with codebook performance assessed using bit error rate (BLER) metrics.

Surface currents, defined as steady flows of energy or particles on a system's boundary that persist despite being out of equilibrium, are a key feature of non-Fermi liquid states within the three-dimensional (3D) Hofstadter model. These 3D surface currents are driven by a mechanism analogous to the 2D surface charge currents associated with the integer quantum Hall effect, yet they operate without requiring a non-zero Hall conductivity. This distinction arises because the energy and particle dispersion curves in this model exhibit a specific symmetry: they are identical for all momentum directions within any given energy shell.

This study examines the rate of mass loss in the Bondi accretion framework, which is defined by the equation $\dot{M} = \frac{\pi e^2 c_s^4}{G P_\infty}\left[1 - \frac{GM}{r_c v_\infty^2} - \left(1 - \frac{G M}{r_c v_\infty^2}\right)^{1/2}\right]$. By analyzing the term within the square brackets, we establish the inequality $\dot{M} \leq \frac{4 \pi e^2 c_s^4}{G P_\infty}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the maximum mass loss rate occurs when the critical radius $r_c$ is set to $3GM/c_s^2$, a value that coincides with the Bondi radius.

We investigate the gravitational wave signals generated by massive binaries within the remnants of Population III stars located in nuclear star clusters. Our findings indicate that the merger rates of these systems are highly sensitive to the efficiency of supernova kicks and the metallicity levels of the early universe. Specifically, stronger kicks and lower metallicities result in significantly reduced merger rates. Furthermore, the characteristic frequency of the emitted gravitational waves is determined by the orbital separation, which in turn depends on the initial stellar mass and the history of binary interactions. We observe that the strongest signals arise from systems where the progenitor stars were more massive, as these stars experience less mass loss and retain tighter post-supernova orbits. Our analysis reveals that the cumulative gravitational wave background from such binaries could reach an amplitude of $\Omega_{\rm GW} \sim 10^{-10}$, a level potentially detectable by future space-based observatories like LISA.

The Gamma-Ray Burst Explorer with two Magnetometers (GECAM) is a dual-satellite mission designed to investigate gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) and other high-energy transients. A key component of GECAM is its Gamma-Ray detector, which consists of 16 scintillator modules. A significant challenge in testing this detector is the difficulty of replicating the extreme radiation environment of gamma-ray bursts in a laboratory setting. To address this, we have developed a portable Gamma-Ray Surge simulator. This device utilizes a high-power, short-pulse electron beam to generate intense, broadband, quasi-white gamma radiation. This setup enables comprehensive on-site testing of the GECAM detector. We report here the design and performance evaluation of the simulator, demonstrating its capability to deliver a peak photon flux of approximately $1.0 \times 10^{11} \, \text{cm}^{-2} \, \text{s}^{-1}$ within a 1 MeV energy range. This paper investigates semigroups of composition operators acting on spaces of analytic functions within the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$. The authors establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the uniform boundedness of $C_{\phi}(t)$ in $\text{BMOA}(\alpha)$, covering both cases where the parameter $\alpha$ is zero and non-zero. Furthermore, they analyze the mean square boundedness of $C_{\phi}(t)$ within $\text{BMOA}(\alpha)$, providing specific criteria for each sub-case. The study extends to the mean Ces`aro-Coppola property, deriving characterization results for the semigroup generated by $C_{\phi}(t)$ when $C_{\phi}(t)$ possesses this property in the specified function spaces. Finally, the paper addresses the mean Ces`aro-Coppola property for integral operators $T_{\sigma}$, deriving sufficient conditions under which $T_{\sigma}$ satisfies this property in $\text{BMOA}(\alpha)$, with particular focus on the case $\alpha = 0$.

This study examines the relationship between scientific productivity and knowledge accumulation, analyzing data from over 1.5 million researchers across 100 nations. We observe that the distribution of publications per individual follows a power law with a slope of approximately -2.2, indicating that roughly 10% of researchers produce 90% of the total output. Assuming a direct link between publication volume and knowledge gained, this would imply a similarly skewed distribution of knowledge among scientists. However, our analysis reveals that the distribution of knowledge is significantly more uniform, with a power law slope of -1.3. This disparity suggests that a researcher's total knowledge is not solely determined by their publication count but is also substantially influenced by collaboration with peers, thereby challenging the conventional "lone genius" narrative.

This paper introduces a physical layer security framework for multi-carrier systems, utilizing amplify-and-forward (AF) relays to enhance data transmission rates while maintaining secrecy against eavesdroppers. The work defines the secure transmission rate for each carrier and derives the optimal power allocation strategy that maximizes the overall secure transmission rate within the network. Furthermore, an efficient algorithm is proposed to solve the associated non-convex optimization problem. Finally, simulation outcomes are presented to validate the system's performance and verify the effectiveness of the suggested algorithm.

In multi-mode quantum electrodynamics within waveguides, integrating a one-dimensional topological structure allows for the creation of resonators with localized defect modes. This paper investigates the dynamics of a two-level system interacting with the field in such an environment. We demonstrate that coupling to a single defect mode yields phenomena such as the Autler-Townes effect, electromagnetically induced transparency, and Fano resonances. Furthermore, coupling to both defect and propagating modes enables the generation of non-Markovian dynamics and the formation of nonlocal entangled states between the atom and the field.

Navigating urban intersections is a core challenge for connected automated vehicles (CAVs), particularly when sharing the road with human-driven vehicles (HDVs). This study proposes a novel, safety-focused, and data-driven predictive control framework for CAVs at signalized intersections with mixed traffic. First, we develop a safety-oriented driving behavior model for HDVs using a supervised learning approach. This model forecasts the future trajectories of nearby HDVs based on current states and traffic light phases, effectively capturing their potential safety risks. Subsequently, we formulate a predictive control scheme that integrates this HDV behavior model with a longitudinal controller and a lateral lane-changing controller. This controller determines the optimal longitudinal speed and lateral lane-switching decisions for a single ego-vehicle to maximize safety and comfort. Finally, we validate the proposed framework through extensive simulations, demonstrating its efficacy in enhancing both safety and comfort for automated vehicles in complex, real-world driving scenarios.

We introduce TextWorldExpress, a high-performance simulation environment for the TextAdventures genre, designed to achieve a one-million-step throughput on a single CPU core. To enable this unprecedented speed, we developed a domain-independent, data-driven approach that compiles game logic into highly optimized C++ code. This method eliminates the need for complex hand-written simulators, a common bottleneck in existing systems. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive platform supporting over 200 games, featuring an intuitive interface for creating new simulations and a robust API for executing natural language commands.

This paper presents a novel algorithmic and hardware co-design for Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, focusing on video recognition tasks. We introduce a hierarchical Tucker tensor-based matrix factorization method designed to compress the weight matrices and bias vectors inherent in standard LSTM architectures. By applying this factorization, we develop an efficient, factorized LSTM (fLSTM) that maintains high recognition accuracy while significantly reducing memory bandwidth consumption. Furthermore, we propose a dedicated hardware accelerator optimized to execute the fLSTM efficiently. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that the proposed fLSTM outperforms existing factorized variants, delivering a 1.6× improvement in energy efficiency and a 1.2× improvement in computational performance.

Data augmentation has become a standard technique for boosting model performance in natural language processing (NLP) by expanding training datasets. While highly effective when data is abundant, its efficacy with limited datasets remains under-explored. This study investigates the utility of data augmentation in low-data NLP scenarios. We utilize three public benchmark datasets to evaluate various augmentation strategies, utilizing a unified framework to ensure consistent evaluation. Our findings indicate that augmentation techniques transferability across different datasets, with their effectiveness varying significantly based on the specific domain.

We introduce a new criterion, termed the Feeble Gravity Conjecture, which posits that for any extremal charged extremal operator in a CFT, the magnitude of its U(1) charge must exceed a specific multiple of its scaling dimension. This criterion is derived from the necessity of maintaining a positive-entropy area law within extremal black holes. We demonstrate that this conjecture holds true for the class of extremal operators arising from the extremal limits of extremal AdS/CFT duality.

We propose a model-space quantum fictitious time evolution method designed to execute stochastic quantum simulations within a restricted model subspace. By integrating model-space quantum Monte Carlo techniques with the imaginary time evolution of model-space amplitudes, this approach facilitates stochastic projections of the wave function onto a specific model space. This framework enables the computation of ground and excited state energies, as well as ground state wave functions, for systems where the model-space quantum amplitude evolves fictitiously in time.

This work establishes that the tight Hilbert polynomial associated with $R$ relative to $\mathfrak{m}$, denoted $ph_T(R|\mathfrak{m})$, coincides with the Hilbert polynomial $ph_T(R|\mathfrak{m})$ of $R$ with respect to $\mathfrak{m}$. This paper introduces an Auxiliary Services Acquisition Model designed to evaluate how market interactions influence the optimal scheduling of grid support, specifically focusing on frequency regulation. The model adopts a bi-level structure where the upper tier represents a Unit Commitment and Scheduling problem aimed at minimizing total system generation costs while adhering to technical constraints, and the lower tier captures market reactions via a power flow solution. By integrating these layers, the approach offers a comprehensive framework for analyzing market responses to support schedules. The study examines various regulatory designs for frequency regulation, contrasting centralized pooling mechanisms with decentralized bidding strategies. Results indicate that accounting for dynamic market interactions is crucial for determining the most effective support schedules. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that the optimal regulation schedule is highly sensitive to the specific design of the support mechanism.

This paper examines the composition $P \circ Q$ of two polynomials with complex coefficients, where the degree of $n = \deg(P \circ Q)$ is a prime number greater than 2. It is demonstrated that if the set of iterates $\{ (P \circ Q)^{\circ k} : k \in \mathbb{N} \}$ generates only a finite number of distinct polynomial degrees, then $n$ must equal the prime number itself. Furthermore, a complete classification is provided for all such pairs $(P, Q)$ under this condition.

The LHCb experiment's unique capabilities in identifying b-flavored jets and distinguishing signal from background make it an ideal environment for searching for Higgs boson pair production decaying into two b-jets and two W bosons ($\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$). This analysis employs a rigorous matrix element method to evaluate the signal significance, utilizing a Monte Carlo simulation of $\textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ events generated via the POWHEG framework. The study utilizes a sample of $100\,\text{fb}^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity at $\sqrt{s}=13\,\text{TeV}$, assuming a b-quark Yukawa coupling of unity and a Higgs mass of $250\,\text{GeV}$. The analysis reveals that the signal significance reaches $10.2\sigma$ under these conditions.

We examine the potential of future linear colliders to investigate extended scalar sectors by utilizing a combined analysis of precision measurements from $e^+e^- \to Z h$ scattering and Higgs diphoton decays ($h \to \gamma\gamma$). We establish the necessary conditions on the linear collider's energy and luminosity required to disentangle the individual contributions of Standard Model and non-Standard Model particles to the Higgs' diphoton decay width. Specifically, we demonstrate that with a center-of-mass energy of 500 GeV and an integrated luminosity of 2 ab$^{-1}$, the masses of additional scalars can be reconstructed with a precision of approximately 1 GeV. This capability allows for a comprehensive probe of various extensions, including the inert two-Higgs-doublet model, $\lambda$-extended scenarios, the singlet-doublet model, and the minimal supersymmetric standard model.

Saturn's stratosphere is characterized by polar seasonal cycles that include the formation of long-lived summertime vortices, a phenomenon that parallels Earth's but differs in the absence of wintery cirrus clouds over the poles. Utilizing high-resolution visible-light imaging from the Keck II telescope, we examined Saturn's northern polar region during the 2019 northern equinox. Our observations revealed a hexagonal structure in the stratosphere that encloses the emerging polar vortex, a feature exhibiting a rotational period identical to the planet's rotation. This finding indicates that the formation of these vortices and associated hexagons occurs within the stratosphere, distinct from the visible cloud layer.

This study examines the mass-supercritical focusing nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation within a domain defined by the outer region of a bounded obstacle. We establish the existence of immediate blow-up solutions for any initial data whose $L^2$-norm strictly exceeds that of the system's ground state. Furthermore, we demonstrate that instantaneous blow-up occurs whenever data is concentrated near a concentration profile associated with the ground state, even if its total mass falls below the critical threshold.

This paper presents the first demonstration of a local uniform reduction applicable to all positive-characteristic semi-parametric algebraically closed fields. It establishes that within varieties defined over finitely generated $\mathbb{Q}$-algebras, every irreducible component of every connected component of the smooth locus is entirely defined by a rational parameter. The core methodology involves a novel semi-parametric variant of the Grothendieck-Lefschetz trace formula, which facilitates the identification of rational subfields through the analysis of $\ell$-adic cohomology.

The transition from a paramagnetic metallic state to a magnetically ordered insulating state in bulk vanadium trisoxide (V$_2$O$_3$) is driven by a strong electron-electron interaction. While doping and strain engineering have been effective in manipulating this metal-insulator transition (MIT) in bulk materials, its behavior in ultrathin films remains less understood. This study demonstrates that surface modification via oxygen adsorption on V$_2$O$_3$(0001) films drastically alters the MIT. Specifically, adsorbed oxygen induces a transition from a low-temperature antiferromagnetic state to a high-temperature ferromagnetic state, accompanied by a shift in the transition temperature ($T_c$) from 17 K to 110 K. Furthermore, the magnetic properties of the films are highly tunable through the thickness of the vanadium layer. Our findings suggest that surface engineering offers a viable pathway to control the MIT in vanadium-based systems.

We investigate the dynamics of quantum dark matter within the nonlinear nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NLSE) by examining stationary, localized, double-dark-soliton solutions. Our analysis reveals that these solitons consist of two distinct branches: a high-energy branch characterized by a large inter-soliton distance and a low-energy branch with a smaller separation. A smooth transition between these branches occurs along a separatrix defined by a critical dark-matter density. Furthermore, we observe that the high-energy branch is highly sensitive to quantum fluctuations, whereas the high-density, low-separation dark matter tends to evolve into the stable, low-energy branch.

Additionally, we examine the phenomenon of Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) in a system of interacting bosons described by the Lieb-Liniger model under precise finite-size scaling conditions. Our findings indicate that the Lieb-Liniger model, when subjected to strict finite-size scaling, accurately predicts the critical density required for BEC in the Lieb-Liniger system.

We introduce the concept of a graded polarization for graded bundles, which serves as a conormal bundle analog. Our investigation focuses on the correspondence between these structures and specific types of degree $2$ degree-$2$ differential operators.

The creation of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP), a deconfined state of QCD matter, was first achieved in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. Since then, experimental efforts have focused on characterizing this QGP phase and the hadron-rich fluid that follows it. This study proposes utilizing resonant x-ray scattering to analyze the nuclear matter produced immediately after the hadronic stage. The analysis indicates that such x-ray scattering experiments are feasible with current technology, potentially offering a novel method to investigate the structural properties of final-state nuclear matter.

This study introduces a novel analytical framework to determine the minimal quantum circuit depth required for error correction between two arbitrary logical qubit configurations. By mapping quantum operations and error structures onto classical statistical models, we derive rigorous lower bounds for circuit depth. Specifically, we demonstrate that the minimal depth corresponds to the shortest path traversing a percolation network, where connectivity is defined by the interaction patterns of Clifford gates. Leveraging this theoretical limit, we analyze the feasibility of implementing quantum error correction across various architectures, including those utilizing fixed-grid two-dimensional surface codes and diverse sets of non-Clifford gates.

Topological insulators and superconductors are categorized by their symmetry-protected topological invariants and gapless surface states, with research increasingly focused on two-dimensional (2D) topological chalcogenides and their functionalized derivatives. This study introduces functionalized 2D tellurene as a candidate for a large-gap 2D topological crystalline insulator, characterized by a non-zero second-order topological invariant ($\nu_2=1$). Our first-principles calculations reveal that pristine 2D tellurene is a narrow-gap semiconductor, whereas functionalization with lithium (Li) or fluorine (F) transforms it into a large-gap ($\sim$0.7 eV) narrow insulator. Notably, Li-functionalized tellurene exhibits a large negative second-order magnetoelectric effect ($\alpha^2_{eff} \sim$ 1000 pm/V), surpassing the values of other known 2D topological insulators. Furthermore, Li-functionalized tellurene displays a large negative magnetoresistance ($\sim$ 90% at 2 T), while F-functionalized tellurene supports a narrow-gap ($\sim$ 0.1 eV) narrow superconductivity. These findings suggest that functionalized 2D tellurene holds significant promise for applications in quantum computing and spintronic devices.

This study introduces a hybridized mixed finite element method designed to model single-phase Darcy flow within fractured porous media. This approach incorporates a newly developed discretization technique for the network of fractures, utilizing a standard mixed finite element method applied to the bulk domain. The resulting system achieves a fully coupled solution for both domain and fracture networks. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that this scheme is well-posed and converges with a second-order accuracy in the $L_2$ norm. Furthermore, numerical experiments validate the method's accuracy and highlight its capability to effectively simulate flow scenarios involving complex fracture geometries.

We present a theoretical investigation into a superconducting spin switch utilizing a chiral spiral magnetic layer. Our findings demonstrate that this layer induces a gapless superconducting state, which can be transformed into a gapped state by applying an external magnetic field. Furthermore, the magnitude of the field required for this transition is highly sensitive to the magnetic pitch of the spiral. Additionally, we identify surface Andreev bound states within the resulting gapless regime, predicting the emergence of a zero-bias conductance peak observable in tunneling experiments.

Hypothetical testing serves as a cornerstone of scientific inquiry, with Bayes factors providing a robust method for evaluating competing models. Nevertheless, their practical application is frequently hindered by subjective model specification and computational constraints. To address these challenges, we introduce a systematic workflow designed to facilitate the effective and efficient implementation of Bayes factors. This approach integrates model selection, regularization, and variable inclusion/exclusion strategies to optimize both computational performance and inferential accuracy. We validate this framework through a comprehensive simulation study, demonstrating that these combined methods substantially enhance the reliability of Bayes factor calculations. Furthermore, we apply these methods to a real-world dataset from psychology, illustrating their utility in empirical research.

Discourse markers (DMs) function as connectors that organize discourse by indicating the semantic relationships between clauses, phrases, or sentences. While current automatic classification methods exist, they often overlook the contextual nuances of these markers. To address this gap, we propose DiscSense, a new framework that integrates contextual information to refine the classification of DMs. This system operates in two stages: first, it extracts contextual features from both the local and global environments surrounding the markers; second, it employs a contextualized word embedding model to classify the DMs using these features. We evaluated DiscSense on the CoNLL-2012 shared task dataset, achieving a micro-averaged F1 score of 69.1%, which represents a 3.1% improvement over the previous year's shared task baseline.

Defect-based systems in diamond, particularly the negatively charged nitrogen vacancy (NV) center, are highly valued for their ability to detect magnetic and electric fields with exceptional sensitivity. These defects also function as robust quantum sensors, leveraging the spin of the electron to measure magnetic fields with high precision. Furthermore, they serve as promising candidates for solid-state quantum computing, leveraging the two-level states of the electron spin. A critical factor influencing the performance of these applications is the zero-field photoluminescence (PL) contrast, which directly affects the efficiency of optical readout. This study investigates the temperature dependence of this zero-field PL contrast for the 637 nm emission associated with the NV center. We find that elevated temperatures significantly diminish this readout contrast, a phenomenon that can be modeled by attributing the dark state of the system to a triplet sublevel ($m_s = 0$) with a zero-field splitting of approximately 1.5 GHz.

Supervised learning has recently emerged as a powerful tool for training artificial neural networks, yet its application to biological systems remains uncertain. This study investigates the feasibility of employing backpropagation to train a biologically plausible recurrent neural network (RBN) that models the architecture of the primary visual cortex. We demonstrate that the weight update rules derived from exact backpropagation can be reformulated into a form that aligns with known neurobiological constraints. Specifically, these updates rely solely on point-wise, local information available within individual neurons and their immediate connections, and they utilize only multiplicative operations. Furthermore, the proposed rule guarantees convergence to a stationary point of the training loss function. Experimental results indicate that these local update rules achieve performance comparable to standard biologically unrealistic models.

We employ a large-$N$ sigma-model framework to investigate $SU(N)$ spins on a triangular lattice, utilizing this model to compute the ground-state degeneracy via its topological term. Our findings indicate that while degeneracy is determined by the topological structure for all $N \ge 2$, it is governed by distinct mechanisms for $N \ge 4$. Specifically, we demonstrate that the topological term in the sigma-model fails to accurately capture the degeneracy of $SU(N)$ spins when $N \ge 4$.

We introduce a novel, self-consistent Hartree-Fock method that employs a B-spline basis to determine the ground states of quantum systems under various central potentials. This approach is demonstrated through applications to neutral atoms, finite clusters, and the electron gas. In these scenarios, we establish the method's validity by comparing results with established data from literature and alternative theoretical frameworks. A key advantage of this technique lies in its ability to accurately model systems with low electron counts, such as atoms and small clusters, by utilizing a compact spline basis. This efficiency allows for the rapid and precise calculation of ground-state properties, including total energy, density, and orbital structures. Furthermore, we apply the method to investigate the quantum behavior of finite electron systems near the transition to neutrality, specifically examining how they resemble an electron gas under conditions of extreme positive ionic core potential. Finally, we present a straightforward algorithm for constructing the spline basis tailored to any given central potential.

Explosive synchronization represents an abrupt transition to synchronized states, characterized by hysteresis and explosive growth in behavior, which stands as a significant phenomenon in dynamical systems. While prior investigations have established generic local conditions near the synchronization onset point applicable to various oscillators, a fundamental question remains regarding the broader criteria for explosive synchronization across entire networks. Addressed here is the case where oscillators share an identical natural frequency yet exhibit diverse dynamics. We demonstrate that such systems undergo explosive synchronization if the coupling between them is anti-phase, defined by a negative imaginary component in the coupling coefficient. Conversely, if this imaginary part is positive, indicating anti-anti-phase coupling, the system transitions smoothly. These findings are validated through multiple representative models, including the Rössler, Lorenz, and general second-order oscillators.

We introduce a novel analytical framework for investigating the global optimization landscape of fixed-rank matrix decomposition, specifically addressing the problem of minimizing the Frobenius norm difference between a given matrix and the product of two low-rank matrices. By applying the framework to the Euclidean factorization, we demonstrate that the objective function becomes geodesically convex when restricted to the Stiefel manifold, thereby guaranteeing the existence of a global minimum at any geodesically convex critical point. Furthermore, we establish the equivalence between Euclidean factorization and the Grassmannian formulation, proving that their critical points are isomorphic. These findings collectively confirm that the fixed-rank matrix decomposition problem possesses a globally convex structure, which holds significant implications for the study of fixed-rank matrix optimization and non-convex matrix factorization.

In 1993, Borodin and Grotzsch conjectured that the robust edge chromatic number of any edge 3-connected cubic bipartite graph is at least its chromatic index plus one. This paper presents the first counterexample to that conjecture, comprising such a graph with 1,166,576 vertices where the robust edge chromatic number equals the chromatic index plus one.

This paper explores novel formulas arising from the functional equation of the Dirichlet $L$-function, specifically focusing on new relations between $L$-function values at various rational arguments.

We introduce a novel framework for Beyond Standard Model (BSM) physics wherein the Higgs potential exhibits spontaneous symmetry breaking, generating a mass gap between the vacuum state and the nearest local minimum. This architecture allows heavy BSM particles to exist with masses reaching as high as $10^{23}$ eV, contingent upon the energy scale separating the electroweak vacuum from the unstable minimum. In this scenario, the stability of the Higgs vacuum vacuum is secured by the formation of cosmic strings, which arise whenever the Higgs potential undergoes a phase transition. These strings possess a tension of order the particle mass squared ($m^2$) and function as energy drains, effectively removing particles from the system. Consequently, the cosmic strings ensure that the heavy particles remain kinetically "insecure," preventing them from accumulating in the current universe. We further demonstrate that this framework can be tested through observations of high-energy cosmic rays and gamma rays.

The mechanics of micro-organisms, such as bacteria and protozoa, are significantly influenced by their viscoelastic surroundings. This study examines how front-back geometric symmetry dictates helical swimming behavior in these organisms. Findings indicate that symmetric organisms experience a transition from corkscrew-like motion to sheet-like movement as environmental viscosity shifts. Conversely, asymmetric organisms maintain consistent corkscrew navigation regardless of viscoelastic conditions. Furthermore, the research reveals that the magnitude of deformation induced by varying viscoelasticity has a differential impact on the helical trajectories of asymmetric swimmers compared to their symmetric counterparts.

This study examines a population of firms within a Cournot framework, where each participant determines output to maximize individual profit, taking rival production levels as fixed. We introduce a genetic algorithm algorithm that evolves a distribution of strategies across firms, allowing parameters to adjust dynamically. By applying this method to the well-known Bertrand Paradox, we demonstrate how the approach recovers the result that perfect competition emerges as a limit of many players in the classic model.

The rapid expansion of knowledge sources presents a significant challenge for ontology-based knowledge representation, creating a pressing need for automated methods to extract missing concepts and relationships from unstructured text. This study introduces a novel deep learning framework designed to enrich ontologies by identifying concepts and relations within natural language. The approach employs a dual-stream architecture: one branch utilizes a character-level model to detect named entities, while the other leverages a sentence-level model to detect spans of text that represent specific concepts or relationships. Evaluation using the RE-ONTO dataset demonstrates that this method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

We introduce a novel framework that merges the Ising model with an elector model, creating a framework to examine how local equilibrium emerges within broader non-equilibrium systems. In this hybrid elector-Ising model, elector spins dictate the interaction strength between neighboring Ising spins, with the global elector state governed by a control parameter $\lambda$. Analysis of the system's phase diagram reveals three distinct phases: a low-temperature ferromagnetic phase, a high-temperature paramagnetic phase, and an intermediate critical phase. This middle phase is characterized by Ising long-range order coexisting with elector criticality, sustained by a first-order phase transition. Furthermore, we explore the implications of this model for local equilibrium in non-equilibrium systems.

The airborne transmission of viruses, influenced by factors such as wind and solar radiation, poses a significant challenge to disease control. This study introduces a new computational framework designed to simulate viral dispersion across diverse environmental settings. By integrating this model with real-world meteorological data from a COVID-19 outbreak in Wuhan, the analysis reveals that viral concentrations in the atmosphere were significantly higher than on the ground. Furthermore, the research indicates that viral dispersion patterns were primarily dictated by local weather conditions, with solar radiation playing a critical role in viral inactivation.

This study introduces a systematic evaluation of uncertainty measurement techniques within Scientific Machine Learning (SML). We categorize these methods into two groups: epistemic uncertainties, which stem from limited data, and aleatoric uncertainties, arising from inherent noise. To validate the approaches, we utilize the Molecule Property Prediction (MPP) dataset, a molecular property classification benchmark. Our analysis reveals that SML models often conflate epistemic and aleatoric uncertainties, frequently failing to accurately isolate either. We further observe that current metrics are insufficient for properly evaluating these metrics. Consequently, we propose a set of novel evaluation metrics and demonstrate the efficacy of our framework through a series of experiments.

Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a weighted oriented graph with edge ideal $I(\mathcal{D})$. This paper investigates the typical powers of $I(\mathcal{D})$ by analyzing the connectivity of associated subgraphs and the ideals formed by edges within specific substructures. Furthermore, we derive several formulas for the symbolic powers of $I(\mathcal{D})$ by comparing them with the ideals generated by edges in the underlying oriented acyclic graph of the oriented acyclic components.

We examine the large-$N$ quantum version of the $O(q) \to U(N)$ matrix model, demonstrating that its partition function is equivalent to the $SU(N)$ Wess–Zumino–Novikov–Polyakov (WZW) model with a specific level $k$. This connection is established through a bosonization-fermionization mapping. Additionally, we analyze the finite-$N$ case, showing that it corresponds to a free conformal field theory (CFT) on a Riemann surface with genus $g = (N^2 - 1)/2(k+2)$.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have become the standard for image recognition, yet their susceptibility to adversarial attacks remains a significant concern. This study introduces a rigorous method for detecting hardware faults in ResNet architectures by employing activation range supervision. This approach establishes expected input-output activation ranges for each layer, enabling the identification of anomalies when activations fall outside these bounds. We propose a novel statistical framework to define these ranges, which are then used to compute a confidence score for the system. Our analysis utilizes over 1.5 trillion images to derive these ranges and evaluates the framework's performance on two distinct hardware fault models. Results indicate that this methodology successfully identifies faults with a 99.99% detection rate while maintaining a false positive rate below 0.01%.

The problem of minimizing transaction cycles, first described by A. Schrijver in 1998, involves finding the shortest cyclic sequence of payments required to settle debts among multiple parties. While this cyclic structure represents a fundamental application of the minimum weight perfect matching algorithm on bipartite graphs, a closed-form characterization of these minimum cycles has remained elusive until now. This paper introduces a novel algorithm that efficiently computes the optimal cyclic payment sequence by leveraging a specific application within the Romanian Ministry of Economy.

This paper introduces a 1-parameter family of Jordanian twists applicable to any rational trigonometric crystallographic root system. This extension generalizes the specific 1-parameter twisted Yangian first presented by Basevich and basevich within their study of twisted quantum affine algebras. The authors also establish the 1-parameter twisted Yangian's definition through both presentations and demonstrate that the limiting case at zero parameter recovers the standard rational trigonometric crystallographic root system. Additionally, this paper investigates the 1-parameter twisted dual quantum affine algebras, establishing their rational limits.
